findings.title: attachments() never selects @odata.type but filters on it, so real file attachments are silently dropped
findings.explanation: GraphAttachment.odata_type is populated only from the `@odata.type` JSON key, but this method's `$select` never requests it, so it deserializes to None for every row (Option<T> fields default to None when the key is absent). The filter then requires `odata_type == Some("#microsoft.graph.fileAttachment")`, which is never true, so every attachment is excluded regardless of whether it is a real file attachment. The sibling method `has_unforwardable_attachments` (line 1071, same file) explicitly adds `@odata.type` to its `$select` for the exact same field on the same endpoint — the asymmetry shows the author knows this field needs to be explicitly requested, but omitted it here.
findings.failure_scenario: A user opens any message that has one or more ordinary file attachments (PDF, image, etc.). `attachments()` fetches the attachment collection, but because `odata_type` is never populated, the filter's `Some("#microsoft.graph.fileAttachment")` comparison fails for every item, so the method returns an empty Vec. The UI's attachment list/download panel shows no attachments even though the message clearly has them.

findings.title: All-day event midnight-snap misclassifies forward timezone shifts of 12h+ as backward shifts, landing on the wrong day
findings.explanation: The function's own doc comment concedes the assumption: the zone-conversion shift is claimed to always be '< 12 h', and any resulting hour >= 12 is assumed to mean the wall clock slid backward across midnight from the next day (so it rolls forward a day to compensate). But real IANA/Windows zone offsets range from UTC-12 to UTC+14, so the offset difference between the event's creation zone and the viewing zone can exceed 12 hours in the forward direction too (e.g. Auckland +13 vs. Los Angeles -7 is a 20h difference, Auckland vs. Hawaii -10 is 23h). A forward shift of, say, 20h from midnight lands at 20:00 the *same* calendar day (no date rollover happened at all), but the hour>=12 heuristic can't distinguish that from a backward shift and incorrectly rolls the date forward by one day.
findings.failure_scenario: A user in Auckland creates an all-day event for July 10. A colleague viewing the agenda from Los Angeles (offset difference 20h) fetches calendarView with Prefer: outlook.timezone="America/Los_Angeles"; Graph returns the same UTC instant as local wall-clock 2026-07-10T20:00:00 (still July 10, just shifted forward within the day). `snap_all_day_to_midnight` sees hour=20>=12 and rolls the date forward to July 11, so the colleague's agenda shows the all-day event one day later than it actually is.
